questions.question: And from ancillary services over 2025-10 to 2026-09, for the 4-hour battery with perfect foresight at ERCOT's hub average, in USD per kW?
questions.answer:
Ancillary-service revenue for the 4-hour battery with perfect foresight at ERCOT HB_HUBAVG, summed over the 12 local months 2025-10 to 2026-09, is 26.80 USD/kW of rated power (26,803.61 USD/MW). This is the sum of the 12 monthly values of foresight_4h_revenue_ancillary_usd_per_mw (battery_stack_monthly, derived). The tool gave the USD/kW figure directly as value_usd_per_kw, 26.803606. No days were left out in any of the 12 months.

The monthly figures ranged from 0.97 USD/kW in 2026-02 to 6.65 USD/kW in 2026-01 (battery_stack_monthly). The mean month was 2.23 USD/kW (battery_stack_monthly).

Perfect foresight is an upper bound, and the battery is modelled as a price taker, so the figures are overstated. The figure covers ancillary services only, with no energy revenue and no capacity payment.

That is the sum of 12 monthly rows of energy plus ancillary revenue, variable dayahead_2h_revenue_total_usd_per_mw; the sum is 51,067.14 USD/MW, and the table gives it as 51.067142 USD/kW. The mean month was 4.26 USD/kW (4,255.60 USD/MW). January 2026 was the highest month at 11.33 USD/kW, and February 2026 the lowest at 2.20 USD/kW. No days were left out in these months. The figures are a modelled upper-bound style estimate with no capacity payment, and the battery is assumed to be a price taker. Months are local (America/Chicago).

# CAISO: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The California Independent System Operator (CAISO) runs the high-voltage grid for most of California and a small part of Nevada. It is a nonprofit grid operator: it owns no power plants, schedules the plants that others own, keeps supply equal to demand, and runs the wholesale market. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules, and California's energy agencies set the state's energy policy. Some California utilities, such as the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power and the Sacramento Municipal Utility District, run their own balancing areas outside CAISO.

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/about ; https://www.caiso.com/about/our-business ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

CAISO runs a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes at the price of that moment. Prices are set at each location (locational marginal prices). Trading hubs summarize them: NP15 in the north, ZP26 in the middle and SP15 in the south; this page uses SP15. CAISO also runs a real-time market for utilities across the West, which lets them trade power with California every few minutes.

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/about/our-business ; https://www.westernenergymarkets.com/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

Sunshine. California produces more solar electricity than any other state (EIA, https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/solar/where-solar-is-found.php), so in the middle of a sunny day the grid can have more power than it needs: prices fall, sometimes below zero, and some solar is turned off (curtailed). When the sun sets, solar output drops just as people come home, and other plants and batteries must ramp up quickly. This evening ramp is why California has built so many batteries, which charge at midday and discharge in the evening: you can see that daily cycle in the battery block on this page.

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/todays-outlook ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/CISO

## A short history

- **1998-03-31:** CAISO begins operating the grid, after California restructured its electricity industry (CAISO, https://www.caiso.com/documents/rtofiling.pdf).
- **2014-11-01:** The Western Energy Imbalance Market starts, letting utilities outside California trade power with CAISO in real time (CAISO, https://www.caiso.com/content/monthly-market-performance/dec-2022/western-energy-imbalance-market.html).
- **2020-08-14:** During a West-wide heat wave, CAISO orders rotating outages because demand outran the power available (CAISO, https://www.caiso.com/Documents/Final-Root-Cause-Analysis-Mid-August-2020-Extreme-Heat-Wave.pdf).

Sources: https://www.caiso.com/about ; https://www.westernenergymarkets.com/

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports CAISO as balancing authority CISO.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price. SP15 is Southern California's.
- **Curtailment:** turning down solar or wind that could have produced, because the grid cannot use or move the power.
- **Evening ramp:** the fast rise in other generation needed as solar output falls at sunset.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.caiso.com/todays-outlook

# MISO: the written layer

## What this grid is and who runs it

The Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) runs the power grid and wholesale market across much of the middle of the country, from Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan south through Iowa, Illinois, Indiana and Missouri to Arkansas, Mississippi, Louisiana and East Texas, and into the Canadian province of Manitoba (MISO, https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/). It owns no power plants: it schedules the plants that its members own, keeps supply equal to demand, and plans transmission. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approves its market rules.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

## How its market sets prices

MISO runs a day-ahead market, where power for each hour of tomorrow is bought and sold today, and a real-time market, where plants are dispatched every few minutes. Prices are set at each location (locational marginal prices) and summarized at trading hubs; this page uses the Indiana Hub. MISO also holds a yearly capacity auction for the coming planning year.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/

## What makes it different

The north-south seam. MISO grew in two parts: the original northern footprint, and MISO South (Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and East Texas), which joined in 2013. The two are tied together by a narrow set of transmission links, so power often cannot flow freely between north and south, and prices on each side can differ. The north has a lot of wind and coal; the south has more natural gas and nuclear.

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/ ; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/dashboard/electric_overview/balancing_authority/MISO

## A short history

- **2001-12-20:** The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approves MISO as the first regional transmission organization (RTO) in the United States (MISO, https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/industry-foundations/miso-history/).
- **2005-04-01:** MISO opens its day-ahead and real-time energy markets (FERC, https://ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/miso-06-30-05.pdf).
- **2013-12-19:** Utilities in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and East Texas join MISO as MISO South (FERC, https://ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/E-4_84.pdf).

Sources: https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/

## Glossary

- **Balancing authority:** the organization that keeps supply and demand equal in an area. EIA reports MISO as balancing authority MISO.
- **Regional transmission organization (RTO):** a grid operator that runs transmission and markets across several states.
- **Demand:** how much electricity customers are using, in megawatts (MW).
- **Megawatt (MW) and megawatt-hour (MWh):** a megawatt is a rate of power; a megawatt-hour is one megawatt for one hour, an amount of energy.
- **Net generation:** the power plants produce, minus what they use themselves.
- **Day-ahead market:** trades for each hour of tomorrow, agreed today.
- **Real-time market:** the price paid for power at the moment it is delivered.
- **Hub:** an average of many grid locations' prices, used as one reference price; this page uses the Indiana Hub.
- **Seam:** a boundary between parts of the grid where power cannot flow freely.
- **Carbon intensity:** the carbon dioxide released per megawatt-hour of electricity, in kilograms of CO2 per MWh.

Sources: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/about ; https://www.misoenergy.org/meet-miso/about-miso/

Hubs: ERCOT HB_HUBAVG, CAISO TH_SP15_GEN-APND, NYISO N.Y.C., MISO INDIANA.HUB, SPP SPPNORTH_HUB, ISO-NE .H.INTERNAL_HUB (the price board's main hubs). PJM is not here: its prices are internal. Wholesale energy only: no transmission, distribution, capacity, ancillary charges or taxes.

Load-weighted: sum over the month's hours of the hour's price x the BA's demand, over the sum of demand; simple: the mean of the same hours; shape premium: load-weighted minus simple (each rounded to 4 decimals first). A month is complete when rt_hours equals hours_in_month; the others are partial and say so on the page.

questions.question: What was the load-weighted real-time price at PJM's Western hub in August 2026, in USD per MWh?
questions.answer: Not in the warehouse. It holds no PJM energy prices (day-ahead or real-time), so there is no PJM Western hub price. The load-weighted cost-of-power table (cost_of_power_monthly) covers only CAISO, ERCOT, ISO-NE, MISO, NYISO and SPP, and no PJM hub series exists. I am stating no figure.
